title: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
hook: a king who reached the highest goal without leaving the palace
tomorrow: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma in chapter three: nobody stays a moment without acting, and action done as offering keeps the wheel turning.

Janaka was a king. He had a palace, a court, a kingdom to run: taxes, quarrels, harvests. And the Hindu tradition remembers him as a sage, someone who knew the Self while sitting on a throne. Halfway through chapter three, Krishna reaches for his name. Janaka and others like him, he says, reached perfection through action itself. Not by walking away. By doing the work. It opens the second half of the chapter, and a word that holds the whole world together.
screen: `JANAKA: A KING AND A SAGE.` → `PERFECTION THROUGH ACTION.` → `A WORD THAT HOLDS THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: The word is lokasangraha. Loka is the world, the people in it. Sangraha is a holding together, a gathering. Krishna tells Arjuna to act with that in view. Then he gives a very human reason. Whatever a leading person does, others do too. Whatever standard they set, the world follows. So the way you work isn't private. Somebody is watching. Then Krishna points at himself. There's nothing in the three worlds, he says, that I have to do, nothing I lack, nothing to gain. And yet I keep acting. If I stopped, people everywhere would follow my path, and the worlds would fall apart. So the wise should act without attachment, as the unwise act with it, for the sake of holding the world together. And they shouldn't unsettle the minds of people attached to their work; let them keep working, and show them how by example. A few verses later: better one's own dharma, even done imperfectly, than another's done well. Your own place in the holding-together, even if it's clumsy. Commentators weigh this differently. Shankara, who holds that liberation finally comes through knowledge, reads the call to act here as fitting for those still on the way, and as an example for others. Some modern readers took lokasangraha as close to the heart of the whole Gita. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, in his long commentary called the Gita Rahasya, read it that way, as a charge to keep working for the world's welfare. The verses can carry both. Either way, karma here isn't only my action. It's one thread in a cloth that a lot of other people are wearing.
screen: `LOKASANGRAHA: HOLDING THE WORLD TOGETHER.` · `WHAT A LEADER DOES, OTHERS FOLLOW.` · `KRISHNA NEEDS NOTHING, AND STILL ACTS.` · `BETTER YOUR OWN DHARMA, IMPERFECT.` · then, large: `ONE THREAD IN THE CLOTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people who see how you work, a child, a coworker, a younger sibling, a neighbor, and just notice that they're there. Then take one thing you do every day, the dishes, a meeting, a commute, and ask what it teaches without a word, seeing it as one thread in the cloth. If you pray, you can offer that one thread.
Karma. Action done for lokasangraha, the holding together of the world, the way King Janaka did it, and the way Krishna says he does.
Your line: hold the world together. Tomorrow, a teaching with a family tree. Day nine hundred sixty-four, done.

chat.says: Why would Krishna bother acting at all, if he needs nothing?
options: If he stopped, people would follow his example and the world would fall apart.
Because acting is how he earns the good merit that he still lacks.
He acts only to win the war for the Pandavas, and then he stops for good.
chat.meaning: Krishna says nothing in the three worlds is his to gain, yet he keeps acting: if he stopped, people would follow, and the worlds would fall apart.

Janaka.meaning: a king remembered as a sage, perfected through action

lokasangraha.meaning: holding the world together: acting for everyone's welfare

Shankara.meaning: a great teacher of non-duality who wrote a Gita commentary

Gita Rahasya.meaning: Tilak's long commentary on the Gita; rahasya means secret
